summary: Psalm 138 is a thanksgiving spoken in the first person. The speaker thanks Yahweh for answered prayer, imagines the kings of the earth joining that praise, and ends by trusting Yahweh to preserve him in trouble and complete what concerns him.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how a short thanksgiving psalm can move from private rescue to public and even worldwide praise. In Book V of Psalms, it adds one more voice of trust before the collection’s final movement toward praise.

context.author: The heading says “By David,” but Psalms headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or collection, and their exact force is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: Individual psalms come from different periods, from the monarchy through later anthology formation; one firm date for this psalm cannot be established from the chapter alone.
context.setting: The poem is oriented toward worship, naming Yahweh’s holy temple, but it does not give a specific historical occasion.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic thanksgiving and trust, using parallel lines, direct address to God, and a movement from personal praise to wider recognition.

outline.heading: Wholehearted praise
outline.note: The speaker gives thanks, sings before the gods, bows toward the holy temple, and praises Yahweh’s Name, loving kindness, and truth.

outline.heading: Answered prayer
outline.note: The speaker remembers calling and being answered with strength in the soul.

outline.heading: Kings will praise Yahweh
outline.note: The poem widens from one worshiper to all the kings of the earth, who hear Yahweh’s words and sing of his ways.

outline.heading: High and lowly
outline.note: Yahweh is described as high, yet attentive to the lowly and distant from the proud.

outline.heading: Trouble and completion
outline.note: The speaker trusts Yahweh to revive, save, fulfill what concerns him, and not forsake the works of his hands.

keyVerses.text: In the day that I called, you answered me. You encouraged me with strength in my soul.
keyVerses.why: This is the personal testimony at the center of the thanksgiving: the speaker called, and Yahweh answered.

keyVerses.text: For though Yahweh is high, yet he looks after the lowly; but he knows the proud from afar.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the chapter’s contrast between Yahweh’s greatness and his concern for the lowly.

keyVerses.text: Though I walk in the middle of trouble, you will revive me. You will stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies. Your right hand will save me.
keyVerses.why: The chapter does not pretend trouble has vanished; it voices trust while the speaker still walks in its middle.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh will fulfill that which concerns me. Your loving kindness, Yahweh, endures forever. Don’t forsake the works of your own hands.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse gathers confidence and petition together: Yahweh will fulfill, yet the speaker still asks not to be forsaken.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading says “By David,” so the received psalm is David-associated. Readers differ on whether such headings always function as modern author bylines; they can also mark association, dedication, or belonging. The voice inside the poem is an individual worshiper who thanks Yahweh for answered prayer.

questions.question: What does “before the gods” mean here?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in the speaker’s opening promise to sing praises to Yahweh. Readers differ on whether “gods” here refers to divine beings, earthly rulers, or another courtly setting; the verse itself does not explain the term. What is clear in the chapter is that the speaker’s praise is directed to Yahweh.

questions.question: Why does the speaker bow toward the holy temple?
questions.answer: Verse 2 presents worship as physically oriented toward Yahweh’s holy temple. Psalms often include temple-oriented worship, but this verse does not describe a full ritual or give a date for the scene. The action is paired with giving thanks to Yahweh’s Name.

questions.question: What does “loving kindness” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: In this translation, “loving kindness” names something about Yahweh that leads the speaker to give thanks. The phrase appears in verse 2 beside “truth” and again in verse 8 as something that “endures forever.” The chapter uses it as a reason for confidence, not as a technical definition.

questions.question: Does verse 4 say every king already praises Yahweh?
questions.answer: No. The verse uses future language: “All the kings of the earth will give you thanks.” The psalm imagines worldwide recognition after the kings hear the words of Yahweh’s mouth, but it does not narrate that event happening inside the chapter.

questions.question: How can Yahweh be “high” and still look after the lowly?
questions.answer: Verse 6 holds both claims together. Yahweh’s greatness does not make him inattentive; the poem says he “looks after the lowly.” At the same time, it says he knows the proud “from afar,” creating a contrast between lowliness and pride.

questions.question: Is the speaker already safe in verse 7?
questions.answer: Not completely. The speaker says, “Though I walk in the middle of trouble,” so danger remains part of the present picture. The verse expresses trust that Yahweh will revive and save, not a claim that trouble has already disappeared.

questions.question: Who are the enemies in this psalm?
questions.answer: Verse 7 mentions “my enemies” and “the wrath of my enemies,” but it does not identify them. In Psalms, enemies can be military, social, legal, or personal, but this chapter does not specify which kind. The main point here is Yahweh’s saving action against their wrath.

questions.question: Why does the final line ask Yahweh not to forsake the works of his own hands?
questions.answer: The closing line turns confidence into petition. The speaker has just said that Yahweh will fulfill what concerns him and that Yahweh’s loving kindness endures forever, yet he still asks not to be forsaken. The chapter therefore ends with trust that remains prayerful rather than self-sufficient.

glossary.def: A term in verse 1 before whom the speaker says he will sing praises to Yahweh; its exact reference is debated.
The place toward which the speaker bows in verse 2 while giving thanks to Yahweh’s Name.
A quality of Yahweh named in verses 2 and 8; in this chapter it grounds thanksgiving and confidence.
Those whom verse 6 says Yahweh looks after, in contrast with the proud.
The saving hand named in verse 7, where the speaker trusts Yahweh to act in trouble.
